facts.fact: A simple random sample of about 1,000 people gives a margin of error of roughly plus or minus 3 percentage points for the whole sample's results.
facts.hook: a student newspaper editor deciding whether a 1,000-person poll is big enough to headline

facts.fact: Bigger samples help less than people expect: doubling a random sample from 1,000 to 2,000 people shrinks the margin of error by only about one percentage point.
facts.hook: a campaign volunteer who wants to double the phone calls to 'make the poll accurate'

facts.fact: A poll's stated margin of error applies to each candidate's share; the margin of error for the lead between two candidates is about twice as large.
facts.hook: a friend who says a 4-point lead with a 3-point margin of error is a sure thing

facts.fact: A subgroup inside a poll has a larger margin of error than the whole poll: 200 people out of a 1,000-person sample carry a margin of about plus or minus 7 points.
facts.hook: a reporter tempted to headline what young voters think from a small slice of a poll

facts.fact: The margin of error measures only random sampling error; it does not cover errors from badly worded questions, people refusing to answer, or poorly conducted interviews.
facts.hook: a student who writes a loaded survey question and trusts the margin of error anyway

facts.fact: For the same sample size, a poll's margin of error is largest when opinion is split near 50 percent, and pollsters usually report that largest figure.
facts.hook: a class survey where one question is nearly unanimous and another is split down the middle

facts.fact: Weighting a poll so its sample matches the population's age, sex or education makes it less biased but also increases the margin of error, an increase statisticians call the design effect.
facts.hook: a stats club noticing their weighted results have a wider margin than the textbook formula

facts.fact: The margin of error only applies to probability samples, where everyone has a known chance of being picked; it does not apply to opt-in online polls that anyone can choose to answer.
facts.hook: a website poll with 50,000 clicks being quoted with a margin of error

facts.fact: In 1936 the Literary Digest poll collected about 2.4 million responses yet predicted that Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt, who then won in a landslide.
facts.hook: a student arguing that a huge online survey must be right because so many people answered

facts.fact: When a candidate's lead is smaller than the margin of error, the poll cannot say with confidence who is ahead, but that does not mean the race is exactly tied.
facts.hook: two friends at a campaign office arguing whether 'within the margin of error' means a tie

facts.fact: A margin of error is expressed in percentage points, not percent: plus or minus 3 points on a 58 percent result means a likely range of 55 to 61 percent.
facts.hook: a student newspaper draft that writes the margin of error as '3 percent of 58 percent'

facts.fact: In the 1948 US presidential race, pollster Elmo Roper declared Thomas Dewey almost as good as elected in September and largely stopped polling, missing a late shift toward Harry Truman, who won.
facts.hook: a campaign team that stops tracking opinion a month before a school election

facts.fact: 'Bottom Line Up Front', or BLUF, is a US military writing standard that puts the main point or request in the first lines of a message, before the supporting details.
facts.hook: a part-time worker rewriting a rambling email to a manager so the request comes first

facts.fact: Barbara Minto, the first woman hired as an MBA by McKinsey & Company, developed the Pyramid Principle: state the main conclusion first, then group the supporting arguments beneath it.
facts.hook: a student organizing a volunteer report that keeps burying its recommendation on page three

facts.fact: An 'I-message', popularized by psychologist Thomas Gordon, states the speaker's own concern, such as 'I'm worried we'll miss the deadline', instead of accusing the listener with 'you' language.
facts.hook: a teen drafting a reply to a coworker who keeps leaving shifts early

facts.fact: Studies of conflict have found that accusatory 'you' statements provoke more anger and more hostile replies than assertive statements describing the speaker's own view.
facts.hook: a volunteer whose blunt 'you never check the schedule' email starts an argument

facts.fact: In his 2013 book Intuition Pumps, Daniel Dennett advised that before criticizing a view you should restate it so fairly that its holder says, 'Thanks, I wish I'd thought of putting it that way.'
facts.hook: a student preparing to disagree with a supervisor's plan in a meeting

facts.fact: Paul Graham's 2008 essay 'How to Disagree' ranks disagreement in seven levels, from name-calling at the bottom to refuting the other person's central point at the top.
facts.hook: a heated group-chat argument about a volunteer event that keeps sliding into insults

facts.fact: A 2005 study by Justin Kruger, Nicholas Epley and colleagues found that email writers overestimate how well readers will pick up their intended tone, such as sarcasm or seriousness.
facts.hook: a joking email to a new manager that gets read as rude

facts.fact: Messages written entirely in capital letters are widely read online and in email as shouting, a convention that spread with bulletin boards in the 1980s.
facts.hook: a teen whose all-caps reminder to other volunteers comes across as angry

facts.fact: Recipients in an email's Bcc field are hidden from everyone else, which is why messages to a long list of people who don't know each other often use Bcc to protect their addresses.
facts.hook: a volunteer coordinator about to email fifty parents with every address visible

facts.fact: Plain-language guidance recommends the active voice, in which the subject does the action, as in 'I missed the deadline', because it makes clear who did what.
facts.hook: a part-time worker tempted to write 'mistakes were made' in an apology to a customer

facts.fact: The US Plain Writing Act, signed by President Barack Obama on October 13, 2010, requires federal agencies to write documents for the public in clear, plain language.
facts.hook: a student struggling through a confusing government form while applying for a job

facts.fact: One of Amazon's leadership principles, 'Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit', asks employees to respectfully challenge a decision they disagree with, then commit fully once it is made.
facts.hook: a team member who lost an argument about a project and must decide how to act next

facts.fact: During Diwali, celebrated by Hindus, Jains, Sikhs and some Buddhists, families light small oil lamps called diyas in homes and temples to symbolize light overcoming darkness.
facts.hook: a teen helping relatives set out rows of diyas before guests arrive

facts.fact: The Islamic calendar is lunar and about 10 to 11 days shorter than the solar year, so Ramadan and Eid al-Fitr come roughly 10 to 11 days earlier each year.
facts.hook: a student surprised that Eid falls during exams this year when it was in summer before

facts.fact: Before the Eid al-Fitr prayer, Muslims who can afford it give a set charity called zakat al-fitr for each family member, so that poor families can also celebrate Eid.
facts.hook: a teen helping a parent arrange the family's zakat al-fitr the night before Eid

facts.fact: At a Passover Seder the youngest child present customarily asks the Four Questions from the Haggadah, beginning with 'Why is this night different from all other nights?'
facts.hook: a grade 12 cousin coaching a nervous younger child through the Four Questions

facts.fact: At Lunar New Year, many Chinese families give money in red envelopes to children and unmarried younger relatives, because red is associated with good fortune and warding off evil.
facts.hook: an older teen unsure whether they are still young enough to receive a red envelope

facts.fact: Chinese red-envelope gifts avoid amounts containing the number four, because the word for 'four' sounds like the word for 'death'.
facts.hook: a teen preparing a gift for a younger cousin who nearly puts in forty dollars

facts.fact: For Mexico's Day of the Dead on November 1 and 2, families build home altars called ofrendas with orange marigolds, whose bright color and strong scent are believed to guide souls home.
facts.hook: a teen placing a late grandparent's photo on the family ofrenda

facts.fact: A Hanukkah menorah has nine branches: eight for the nights of the holiday and one for the shamash, the helper candle used to light the others, one more each night.
facts.hook: a teen lighting the menorah on the fourth night and losing count of the candles

facts.fact: A Sikh gurdwara's langar serves free vegetarian meals to anyone regardless of religion, caste or status, and people traditionally eat together seated on the floor as equals.
facts.hook: a teen bringing a non-Sikh friend to a gurdwara celebration for the first time

facts.fact: Many Orthodox churches, including the Russian Orthodox Church, celebrate Christmas on January 7 because they keep December 25 on the older Julian calendar.
facts.hook: a family visiting grandparents who celebrate Christmas two weeks after the neighbors

facts.fact: Kwanzaa, created by Maulana Karenga in 1966, runs from December 26 to January 1 and honors seven principles, one each day, beginning with Umoja, meaning unity.
facts.hook: a teen asked to explain the day's principle at a family Kwanzaa gathering

facts.fact: The Hindu festival of Holi falls on the full moon of the month Phalguna, usually in March, and begins with a bonfire the night before called Holika Dahan.
facts.hook: a teen joining relatives at the Holi bonfire before the next morning's colors

facts.fact: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, set up in 1988 by the World Meteorological Organization and the UN Environment Programme, does no original research; it assesses the published scientific literature.
facts.hook: a student who assumes the IPCC runs its own climate experiments

facts.fact: A meta-analysis combines the results of many independent studies of the same question into one overall estimate; the term was coined by statistician Gene Glass in 1976.
facts.hook: a science fair judge asking why one study isn't enough to settle a question

facts.fact: Andrew Wakefield's 1998 Lancet paper claiming a link between the MMR vaccine and autism described just twelve children, and The Lancet fully retracted it in 2010.
facts.hook: a relative sharing an old article about vaccines at a doctor's office visit

facts.fact: A Danish study published in 2019 followed more than 650,000 children and found no link between the MMR vaccine and autism, even among children with autistic siblings.
facts.hook: a student comparing a twelve-child study with a study of hundreds of thousands

facts.fact: In 2011 the OPERA experiment reported neutrinos apparently faster than light; in 2012 the result was traced to a loose fibre-optic cable, and other experiments measured speeds consistent with light.
facts.hook: a friend excited by a headline claiming one experiment has overturned Einstein

facts.fact: Papers posted on arXiv, the preprint server Paul Ginsparg started in 1991, are checked by moderators for relevance but are not peer reviewed before they appear.
facts.hook: a student citing a preprint as settled science in a science fair report

facts.fact: A 2013 study led by John Cook examined 11,944 climate paper abstracts and found that 97.1 percent of those taking a position endorsed human-caused global warming.
facts.hook: a debate where someone claims scientists are evenly split on climate change

facts.fact: The Higgs boson discovery on July 4, 2012 was announced only after two separate CERN detector teams, ATLAS and CMS, independently found the same new particle.
facts.hook: a museum visitor asking why CERN needed two giant detectors instead of one

facts.fact: Particle physicists claim a discovery only at 'five sigma', meaning there is less than a one-in-a-million chance that a random fluctuation alone would produce a signal that strong.
facts.hook: a student whose experiment shows a small effect wondering how sure is sure enough

facts.fact: Barry Marshall and Robin Warren identified the bacterium Helicobacter pylori as a cause of stomach ulcers in the early 1980s and received the 2005 Nobel Prize for it.
facts.hook: a patient in a doctor's office surprised that ulcers are treated with antibiotics

facts.fact: In 1942 sociologist Robert K. Merton named 'organized skepticism' as a norm of science: claims must survive critical scrutiny by the community before they are accepted.
facts.hook: a student annoyed that classmates keep questioning her science fair result

facts.fact: In 1904 physicist Robert W. Wood secretly removed a key prism from René Blondlot's apparatus, yet observers still reported seeing Blondlot's claimed 'N-rays', showing they were seeing what they expected.
facts.hook: a lab partner who swears the results look better after she knows what to expect

facts.fact: In her 1997 essay on leverage points, Donella Meadows argued that adjusting numbers like taxes or subsidies rarely changes a system much, while changing its goals or underlying paradigm changes the most.
facts.hook: a city council debate that only argues about the size of a parking fee

facts.fact: The Limits to Growth, published in 1972 for the Club of Rome by an MIT team, used a computer model called World3 to link population, food, industry, pollution and resources.
facts.hook: a class project trying to show how a town's growth affects its water supply

facts.fact: In 1902 French authorities in Hanoi paid a bounty per rat tail; people cut off tails, released the rats to breed and even farmed rats, so the rat population grew.
facts.hook: a school council designing a reward that students might game

facts.fact: The Soviet Union diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers to irrigate cotton, and the shrinking, saltier Aral Sea lost a fishing industry that had employed about 40,000 people.
facts.hook: a farm visit where students discuss who downstream loses when water is diverted

facts.fact: China's campaign to kill sparrows, launched in 1958, removed a predator of crop-eating insects, and locust swarms that followed contributed to the Great Chinese Famine.
facts.hook: a community garden debate about getting rid of all the birds eating the seeds

facts.fact: In his 1865 book The Coal Question, William Stanley Jevons observed that more efficient steam engines made coal cheaper to use and increased Britain's total coal consumption.
facts.hook: a student wondering why the town's energy use rose after everyone got efficient bulbs

facts.fact: Sea ice reflects most sunlight while open ocean absorbs most of it, so melting ice exposes darker water that warms and melts more ice: a reinforcing feedback loop.
facts.hook: a science class sketching why Arctic warming speeds itself up

facts.fact: Adding lanes to a congested highway often fails to reduce traffic for long, because faster trips attract more driving until the new space fills; this effect is called induced demand.
facts.hook: a city council meeting where residents push to widen the main road

facts.fact: The 1930s Dust Bowl followed the plowing of the Great Plains' native deep-rooted grasses, which had held the soil, so when drought came the wind carried the topsoil away.
facts.hook: a farm field trip where a farmer explains why she leaves strips of grass

facts.fact: Ireland's Great Famine began in 1845 when potato blight struck a population that relied heavily on one potato variety, the Lumper, whose lack of genetic variety left it vulnerable.
facts.hook: a community garden planning whether to plant just one reliable crop

facts.fact: The 1987 Montreal Protocol, which phases out ozone-destroying chemicals, was the first treaty in United Nations history to be ratified by every UN member state.
facts.hook: a class debating whether countries can ever agree on an environmental problem

facts.fact: A 2020 study of 108 US cities found that neighborhoods once 'redlined' by 1930s housing policy are on average about 2.6 degrees Celsius hotter, largely from fewer trees and more pavement.
facts.hook: students mapping summer temperatures across their city for a school project

facts.fact: Canada's federal Goods and Services Tax, introduced on January 1, 1991 at 7 percent, has been 5 percent since January 1, 2008.
facts.hook: a teen at a part-time job checking the GST line on a customer's receipt

facts.fact: Ontario combines the federal GST with its provincial sales tax into a single 13 percent Harmonized Sales Tax, shown as one HST line on receipts.
facts.hook: a student in Toronto working out why a restaurant bill has only one tax line

facts.fact: The United States has no national sales tax; sales taxes are set by states and local governments, so the rate on a receipt depends on where the purchase is made.
facts.hook: a road-trip snack costing different amounts in two neighboring towns

facts.fact: Five US states, Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire and Oregon, have no statewide sales tax.
facts.hook: a friend planning to buy a laptop across the state line

facts.fact: In the United States and Canada, shelf and menu prices usually do not include sales tax, which is added at the register, so the total is higher than the posted price.
facts.hook: a teen with exactly enough cash for the menu price at a restaurant

facts.fact: The United Kingdom's standard rate of VAT, a sales tax built into most prices, has been 20 percent since January 4, 2011.
facts.hook: a student comparing a UK receipt with a Canadian one online

facts.fact: In the United States, employers withhold 6.2 percent of an employee's wages for Social Security and 1.45 percent for Medicare, shown on pay stubs as FICA or separate lines.
facts.hook: a teen puzzling over why a first paycheck is smaller than hours times wage

facts.fact: In Canada outside Quebec, a typical paycheque shows deductions for income tax, Canada Pension Plan contributions and Employment Insurance premiums; Quebec uses its own pension and parental insurance plans.
facts.hook: a student comparing pay stubs with a friend who works in another province

facts.fact: US employers must generally give each employee a Form W-2 by the end of January, showing the previous year's wages and the taxes withheld, which is needed to file a tax return.
facts.hook: a teen with a summer job waiting for the form needed to file taxes

facts.fact: In many tax systems, a deduction lowers the income that tax is calculated on, while a tax credit subtracts directly from the tax owed, so a credit is usually worth more than an equal deduction.
facts.hook: a student at a computer comparing two tax breaks on a first return

facts.fact: A refundable tax credit is paid out even when it exceeds the tax owed, while a non-refundable credit can only reduce the tax owed to zero, with the rest lost.
facts.hook: a teen with low earnings wondering whether filing a return is worth it

facts.fact: In countries where tax is withheld from pay, such as the US and Canada, a tax refund means more was withheld during the year than was owed; it is an overpayment returned, not extra income.
facts.hook: a friend celebrating a refund as 'free money' at the bank

facts.fact: The world's first food bank, St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, was founded in 1967 by John van Hengel.
facts.hook: a first-time volunteer reading the history poster on the warehouse wall

facts.fact: Canada's first food bank opened in Edmonton on January 16, 1981.
facts.hook: a volunteer surprised that food banks in Canada are only a few decades old

facts.fact: A food bank is usually a central warehouse that collects and distributes food to local agencies, while a food pantry is where people pick up food directly.
facts.hook: a new volunteer confused about why no one visits the warehouse for groceries

facts.fact: Feeding America, founded by John van Hengel in 1979 as America's Second Harvest, is a US network of more than 200 food banks.
facts.hook: a volunteer noticing the same logo on boxes from different cities

facts.fact: A 'best before' date marks when a food's quality may start to decline, not when it becomes unsafe, so sealed food past that date may still be safe to eat.
facts.hook: a first-time sorter about to throw out cans a week past their best-before date

facts.fact: The US Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act of 1996 gives food donors limited protection from liability, which encourages stores and restaurants to donate surplus food.
facts.hook: a restaurant owner explaining why she can safely donate leftover bread

facts.fact: Many food banks cannot accept home-cooked or opened food, because they cannot check how it was prepared or stored.
facts.hook: a volunteer who has to turn away a neighbor's homemade lasagna kindly

facts.fact: Food Banks Canada's HungerCount 2025 recorded nearly 2.2 million food bank visits in Canada in March 2025, a record for a single month.
facts.hook: a volunteer shocked by how long the line is on a weekday

facts.fact: Children accounted for about one-third of food bank visits in Canada in March 2025, according to Food Banks Canada's HungerCount report.
facts.hook: a teen packing hampers who notices how many include baby food and snacks

facts.fact: Ontario high school students must complete 40 hours of community involvement to earn the Ontario Secondary School Diploma.
facts.hook: a grade 12 student logging food bank hours before the diploma deadline

facts.fact: Food-safety guidance says refrigerated food must be kept at or below 4 degrees Celsius (40 degrees Fahrenheit) to slow the growth of bacteria.
facts.hook: a volunteer who finds the donated milk sitting on a warm loading dock

facts.fact: In gleaning programs, food bank volunteers harvest crops that remain in farm fields after the main harvest, food that would otherwise go to waste.
facts.hook: a group of first-time volunteers picking leftover squash on a Saturday morning

facts.fact: The first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967, when the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10 in Los Angeles.
facts.hook: a grandparent at a Super Bowl party claiming to remember the very first one

facts.fact: The 2026 FIFA World Cup, hosted by Canada, Mexico and the United States, was the first with 48 teams and the first hosted by three countries.
facts.hook: friends at a restaurant arguing about how many teams qualified this time

facts.fact: Home teams win more often in most major sports; in the 2018-19 NBA season, home teams won about 59 percent of games.
facts.hook: a family debating whether their team's home-game record means anything

facts.fact: The yellow first-down line shown on televised American football is computer-drawn; it was first broadcast on ESPN on September 27, 1998, by a company called Sportvision.
facts.hook: a younger cousin who thinks the yellow line is painted on the field

facts.fact: The first instant replay on television was shown by CBS during the Army-Navy football game on December 7, 1963, using a system devised by director Tony Verna.
facts.hook: fans at a neighbor's house demanding a replay of a disputed play

facts.fact: The Stanley Cup, donated in 1892 by Lord Stanley of Preston and first awarded in 1893, is the oldest existing trophy awarded to a professional sports team in North America.
facts.hook: a family watching the final game of the playoffs at a grandparent's house

facts.fact: Robert Cialdini's 1976 study found that students wore more university clothing after their football team won and said 'we' more when describing wins than losses.
facts.hook: a friend who says 'we won' after the game though he has never played

facts.fact: A 1985 study by Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky called basketball's 'hot hand' an illusion, but a 2018 reanalysis by Miller and Sanjurjo found a statistical flaw and evidence of streak shooting.
facts.hook: fans arguing whether a player on a scoring run is really 'on fire'

facts.fact: Pierre de Coubertin designed the five Olympic rings in 1913, choosing colors so that every national flag of the time contained at least one of them, including the white background.
facts.hook: a teen watching the Olympics looking for their flag's colors in the rings

facts.fact: The 2018 World Cup in Russia was the first to use video assistant referees, who can review goals, penalties, direct red cards and cases of mistaken identity.
facts.hook: a room full of fans waiting for a VAR check on a late goal

facts.fact: A 2002 study of stadium waves found they usually travel clockwise at about 12 meters, or about 22 seats, per second, and can be started by a few dozen fans.
facts.hook: friends at a community field trying to start a wave in the stands

facts.fact: In soccer, being in an offside position is not an offence by itself; a player is penalized only when involved in active play, and there is no offside from a throw-in, goal kick or corner.
facts.hook: a relative shouting 'offside!' at a goal that came straight from a corner kick
